# R361 — stockbench32K decode24 variance: phase attribution and next diagnostic

Date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Tokyo). Read-only source/report audit for `/home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/yqYo1/Strata/.worktree/diag-native-copy-queue-qualified-20261013`, current qualified `410904c/freeb54579b`, SourceLLVM 7.1.1 / UR v2 / DirectSubmission off. No tests, builds, AST/import, GPU, profiler, process/service query, reset, Git operation, source edit or measurement was performed. Only this report was written. The private `prefill-gemm-only-contract-root-v1/record.json` and broad environment were not read.

## Finding

The quiet three-request stockbench result supplied for the original approximately 32K prompt and 24-token decode is valid as a small sample of end-to-end request variance; it does not localize that variance. The supplied decode rates (9.7, 8.6, 7.9 tok/s) span 1.8 tok/s, but each run has an intentionally different prompt tag and is not an exact paired token-ID history. Different routing can therefore change the CPU expert job mix. The fixed identity result and no-fault status rule out those observed faults as an explanation for these three samples; they do not identify the source of timing spread.

The existing `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` receipt and `--stats` pool counters provide useful coarse localization when collected on the same client/model path. They cannot by themselves separate CPU work from queueing, worker tail, host synchronization or GPU work hidden behind callback intervals. In particular, dispatch section totals, pool phase totals and GPU-reach wait are not independent serial pieces of decode time. Do not apply Amdahl fractions, sum the worker phases into request time, subtract counters from wall, or convert submitted packed bytes into physical RAM traffic.

The quiet COPY0 C0 numbers supplied (prefill 407.5/408/403 ms, decode 9.7/8.6/7.9 tok/s) are retained as the clean baseline. C1 is incomplete in the supplied state (GPU 38,293 active; result records not yet available), so no COPY0/1 conclusion follows. The native copy-only queue is not submitted for ordinary decode; R354 identifies a possible host lookup cost on compute submission under opt-in, but it remains a candidate rather than an attribution. Keep copy mode fixed for the next phase diagnostic.

## Exact source counter boundaries

`src/program/generate.cpp:5867-5885` snapshots `Verifier::{ms_wait,ms_pool,ms_host,ms_commit}` and dispatch `{ms_plan,ms_actq,ms_jobs,ms_run}` at the start of the request decode loop. At `:5900-6003`, `dt_run` is host wall around each `ver.run`; `dt_commit` wraps commit plus token emission/progress output; `dt_draft` wraps MTP draft work. `decode_ms` is measured from before the decode loop to its exit, before the final `ver.wait_commit`; the printed line is emitted after that commit wait. The print reports per-window averages (`windows`, average T, tokens/window), not per-token timing and not individual-token intervals. With the supplied no-MTP, segmented route, the window size is one, so each of 24 tokens generally corresponds to a verify window, subject to actual early stop/status.

The formatted decode line labels `verify` as `GPU-reach wait + per-layer host + stage`. These are the four `Verifier` accumulators `ms_wait`, `ms_pool`, `ms_host`, `ms_commit` in `include/strata/core/verify.hpp:166` and are incremented in `src/core/verify.cpp` (`ms_wait` at `:1327`, `ms_pool` at `:1328`, `ms_host` at `:1223`, commit at `:1625`). `ms_wait` covers the host interval waiting for the GPU to reach a layer boundary (`:1246-1281`); it can include event/scheduling/driver delay and is not GPU execution time. `ms_pool` is elapsed time after that boundary around the CPU expert callback. `ms_host` is verify-window token/position/history staging before graph launch. `ms_commit` is commit launch and, where synchronous, stream synchronization; the configured async path changes that boundary. These values accumulate across window/layer steps and can overlap device execution or other host activity.

`src/core/expert_source.cpp:2111-2114` adds `ms_plan`, `ms_actq`, `ms_jobs`, `ms_run` as adjacent host-clock spans within `expert_pool_dispatch_multi`: planning, activation quantization, grouping jobs, and `run_split_multi[_native]` including completion/return. These dispatch counters are nested inside `ms_pool` / `Drive::cpu_ms` callback time, across repeated layers. The pool's own GU, quantize and Down counters printed at `src/program/generate.cpp:6886-6891` are pool phase wall elapsed values, with worker scheduling/barrier/host participation and potentially simultaneous GPU graph work. They are not per-worker active CPU time, exclusive CPU service, or independent totals to add to request decode.

The decode receipt also prints CPU expert jobs (`multi_misses`), routed entries (`multi_entries`), VRAM hits and PCIe expert counts normalized per layer-window (`generate.cpp:6002`). These are counts, not job cost or physical bytes. `drive_pool_multi` (`generate.cpp:714-730`) invokes dispatch per layer and accumulates the outer callback interval. Under the supplied no-cache/reuse recipe, the counters can describe routing and CPU ownership, but do not show which format/NT mix drove each sample or the slowest worker's remaining work. With cache hit rate around 1.8%, a hit percentage alone is not a sufficient variance explanation.

## What the quiet sample does and does not establish

The 3-run range is a signal to investigate, not proof of a stable effect or a compute bottleneck. Temperature zero removes sampling randomness but does not make the per-run fresh/tagged prompts identical. Prompt token variation can alter selected experts, and distinct selected experts have different formats, native kernels, row counts, and cache/VRAM outcomes. The output also varies by generated content, which can make the observed short horizon's routing differ. No universal generated-text match gate can make this input variation disappear.

Use each stockbench request's actual engine `generated_tokens`, `decode_tps_source`, `prompt_tokens`, prompt read/reused counts, HTTP status and finish result when reviewing the existing records. Keep only valid engine `decode_tps` rows with successful status, nontrivial actual token count and the same stock client/config definition. Do not use client-rate fallback as if it were the engine rate. The max token cap is 24, not a guarantee of 24 output tokens. Three samples are too few to characterize tails; preserve each request row and do not report a pooled average without showing the range and count.

C0 prefill spread (403–408 ms) and decode spread are distinct phases; no evidence supplied shows the prefill difference caused the decode rate spread. The decode starts after the prompt is consumed, with state/context position and routing as conditions. Do not infer decode from whole-request minus prefill because those intervals and stream tails need not share clean boundaries.

## Next same-client diagnostic: minimum useful set

First finish reading the already-produced C1 quiet request records; this adds no run and is necessary to establish whether COPY0/1 has a reproducible delta. If there is no material paired distribution-level difference, do not spend a profiler run on the copy hypothesis. If there is a repeatable delta, retain COPY as a fixed setting for localization and run one bounded diagnostic on the same stockbench client, same model/configuration and same long-row request construction, with `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` and `--stats` enabled. This uses the existing counters only; do not substitute a different harness, shorten the prompt, increase output horizon, or change generation settings. Keep per-request association between the client result row and the corresponding engine stderr timing line. Cap collection at the supplied operational limits: at most 40 minutes and 64 MiB of logs; stop after enough valid long rows to see whether the attribution repeats. Log output must retain request identity/order, model/build/config, actual prompt/generated counts, route/finish/correctness, and both timing lines. Any instrumentation-on numbers are diagnostic and must not replace the timing-off quiet distribution.

For each valid request, compare decode wall/window, window count and T; verify wait; per-layer host and staging; commit/emit; draft; pool callback and its nested plan/activation-quantize/jobs/run spans; pool GU/quantize/Down phases; CPU job/entry counts; cache hit and PCIe expert counts; and the GPU stage line if it is already produced by the source configuration. Keep all measurements in their native denominators. Interpret consistent covariance only: e.g. repeatable decode slowdown with higher wait may indicate exposed device/rendezvous delay, while longer pool callback/dispatch may indicate CPU callback service or its tail. Neither establishes worker imbalance or GPU utilization.

The timing and stats environment controls already exist, but `--stats` aggregates over the broader generation invocation while `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` is request-scoped; on a multi-request server process these scopes must not be silently joined by row unless their request boundaries can be established from existing output. If the client launches an isolated process per request, capture that process association. If it shares a long-lived server and the stats line cannot be mapped to one request, use it only as run-level context and do not claim request-level correlation. Do not add Source counters for this first pass.

## Decision after the existing-counter pass

1. If the same timing component consistently tracks decode wall across valid rows and COPY arms (with worker recipe unchanged), that is evidence to target that source path for a narrowly scoped next design. It is not yet proof of critical-path cost because the counters can be nested/overlapped.
2. If `ms_pool` / dispatch and GU/Down move with decode, but `ms_run` or phase wall is not separable from waiting and GPU work, the next useful diagnostic is aggregated per-worker active duration plus completion-tail/barrier/park duration by pool phase and routed `(layer, expert format, NT)` demand histogram. Record per-worker totals/max and phase request boundaries, not per-job lines. This directly distinguishes useful CPU service, uneven worker completion, and task-queue/barrier tail; it must be separately labelled and checked against quiet runs for perturbation.
3. If verify wait or host staging moves while CPU pool measures are stable, add bounded timestamps only at existing layer completion, pool entry/return, next graph launch, stream wait completion and final verify completion seams. Join them as intervals/dependencies on the host steady clock; do not add event synchronization to every expert or call a wait interval “GPU compute.”
4. If the above still leaves a suspected device stage, use the source's existing GPU stage profile only if it is already available and its clock conversion is validated for this device/runtime. Do not invoke VTune/unitrace or an external profiler as the first diagnostic: no compatibility/collection qualification for this exact LLVM 7.1.1 / UR v2 / B570 setup is established by this read-only audit. An optional profiler is useful only after a bounded standalone compatibility probe is independently admitted and its output can answer a specific unresolved interval.

Avoid running extra 16K/short-input comparisons as a substitute for the original 32K client row: that changes the requested workload and can alter route/position behavior. A later diagnostic may include a matched contextual control only if the exact same client supports it and the question explicitly concerns context sensitivity, but it cannot replace the same-workload measurement.

## Current decision

The supplied evidence does not yet establish that decode variance is caused by CPU work, CPU worker imbalance, GPU execution, host dispatch, native COPY queue guarding, RAM bandwidth, or PCIe service. Complete C1 result review, then use a bounded same-client pass with the existing request decode line and `--stats` to find which counter family covaries. Only add worker active/tail or boundary timestamps if that first pass leaves a specific ambiguity. No change in optimization priority is supported yet.
